issues.legal_issue: A government company’s statutory option to renew a lease is subject to objective, bona fide, and reasonable exercise and is not an unreviewable right to renew merely by expressing a desire to do so.
material_facts: The government company’s predecessor held the premises under a lease, and the company invoked the statutory renewal mechanism for a further term on the existing terms.
The rent remained unpaid during the prolonged litigation, and the company made no proposal to increase it.
Evidence showed that business at the premises had declined after traffic was diverted, and the company did not establish a current need for renewal.
The courts below concurrently found that the company’s desire to renew was not bona fide.
The eviction decree had been executed and possession had been delivered to the owners.
issues.conclusion: The company’s renewal request was not enforceable because its desire to renew was arbitrary and failed the required standard of fairness and reasonableness; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5(2) and 7(3) of the Burmah Shell (Acquisition of Undertakings in India) Act, 1976 create a renewal right for a qualifying lease, and the special Act overrides the general rule in Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. But the statutory expression of a desire to renew requires objective support; a State company within Article 12 must act bona fide, fairly, and reasonably, and its action is subject to judicial review. The Court relied on Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. P. Kesavan for the statutory renewal right; Amarnath Ashram Trust Society v. Governor of U.P., M/s. Dwarkadas Marfatia & Sons v. Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay, Noble Resources Ltd. v. State of Orissa, and State of Karnataka v. All India Manufacturers Organisation for the duty of fair and non-arbitrary State action; M.L. Kamra v. Chairman-cum-Managing Director, New India Assurance Co. Ltd. for constitutionally consistent interpretation; and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai for strict construction of expropriatory legislation and the constitutional status of property rights.

rule.if: government_company_tenant and statutory_lease_renewal_case and renewal_option_invoked and no_evidence_of_current_operational_need and (rent_unpaid_during_litigation or business_at_premises_declined)

predicates.government_company_tenant: A government-owned company held the premises as a tenant.
predicates.statutory_lease_renewal_case: The dispute concerned a tenant’s request to renew a lease under a statutory renewal mechanism.
predicates.renewal_option_invoked: The tenant communicated that it wished to renew the lease.
predicates.no_evidence_of_current_operational_need: The tenant did not establish an objective current need to continue using the premises.
predicates.rent_unpaid_during_litigation: The tenant did not pay rent during the litigation.
predicates.business_at_premises_declined: Evidence showed that business conducted at the premises had declined.

issues.definition: When a government company invokes a statutory lease-renewal option without evidence of a current operational need, and rent went unpaid or business at the premises declined, its desire to renew is not enforceable.
